thread_anchor.heading: Part 2 — Regents Thread Anchor
thread_anchor.label: Primary Thread 1 — Is There One America?
thread_anchor.question: "When the Constitution promises equality, does it mean everyone?"
thread_anchor.question_note: This is the earliest entry in the Thread 1 arc — before there is a Constitution to promise anything.
thread_anchor.lead: How Thread 1 appears in this unit:
points: In 1619, twenty captive Africans sold at Jamestown were classified as indentured servants — the same status as many poor English colonists. The line between the two was not yet built.

Between 1640 and 1705, colonial law built that line, statute by statute: John Punch sentenced to lifelong servitude (1640) while white servants in the same case were not; children inheriting their mother's enslaved status (1662); and finally the 1705 Virginia slave codes, which declared enslaved people real property — legally real estate, with no legal standing as people at all.

Bacon's Rebellion (1676) sits in the middle of that process. Poor whites and enslaved people rebelled together against Virginia's elite — and the colony's response afterward hastened the shift toward hardened racial slavery and away from a shared servant class.
thread_anchor.after: The same era, by a different mechanism, English coverture law absorbed a married woman's legal identity into her husband's — no property, no contracts, no vote. A different group, the same era's answer to "who counts as a full legal person."

background.heading: Background — self-governance and limited government (Thread 3 opens formally in Unit 2, not here)
background.text: The Virginia House of Burgesses (1619) and decades of salutary neglect gave colonists real practical self-governance before 1763 — the expectation Thread 3 will later test directly, once there's a government to build. Worth knowing now; not yet a Thread 3 claim.

key_facts.heading: Part 3 — Key Facts by Block
key_facts.note: Thread connection note: The same year Virginia held its first representative assembly (1619), the first enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia. This tension — freedom claimed for some, bondage imposed on others — runs through every unit in this course.

rows.detail: First representative assembly in English North America. Colonists claimed self-governance as a right of English citizens. Precedent for all future colonial assemblies.
rows.thread: Background — self-governance as an early expectation, tested directly by Thread 3 starting in Unit 2

rows.detail: Both indentured servants and enslaved Africans were bound labor in the 1600s — worked, bought, sold. The legal line between them was built over ~85 years, not found. By 1705, only one group could be bought, sold, and inherited for life.
rows.thread: Thread 1 — the line was built, statute by statute, against people who had no vote in building it

rows.detail: Poor whites and enslaved/indentured Black Virginians rebelled together against the colony's elite. Virginia's response afterward hardened colonial law along racial lines in the years that followed.
rows.thread: Thread 1 — shows the moment colonial elites chose race over class as the line to defend

rows.detail: Declared all Black, Mulatto, and Indian enslaved people real property — legally real estate. Forbidden to assault a white person, denied the right to bear arms, denied movement without written permission.
rows.thread: Thread 1 ⚑ — the key document for the African American arc in Unit 11.1

rows.detail: Britain loosely enforced trade laws and let colonial assemblies govern locally for generations. Ended after the French & Indian War when Britain needed revenue.
rows.thread: Background — decades of practical self-rule that made 1763's shift feel like a violation

rows.detail: European goods to Africa; enslaved Africans to the Americas; raw materials to Europe. ~300,000 Africans transported to British North America — the economic foundation of the plantation South.
rows.thread: Thread 1 — slavery built into the colonial economy, not an afterthought to it

exam.heading: Part 4 — Regents Exam Appearances
exam.text: Unit 11.1 content appears most frequently in Part I (Multiple Choice) as historical context for the Revolution and constitutional founding. The servant/slave comparison and the 1705 slave codes appear as Thread 1 stimulus material in both Part I and Thread 1 CLE essays.

watch_for.cue: Charts or passages comparing indentured servitude and slavery
watch_for.move: look for what has no equivalent on the other side; that's the line the law built
identify the pattern: rights being removed one at a time, not all at once
connect it to why colonial elites shifted toward race-based slavery afterward

watch_for.cue: Passages about colonial assemblies or 'rights of Englishmen'
watch_for.move: background for the Revolution, not yet a Thread 3 claim

three_move.heading: Part 5 — Three-Move Answer Practice
three_move.intro: Write three sentences using the Three-Move Regents Answer framework: (1) Name the promise or principle at stake. (2) Show how it was undermined. (3) Show partial redemption — or note that, this early, there isn't one yet.

moves.move: Move 1 — Name the principle colonists claimed for themselves.
moves.starter: "Colonists who settled Virginia beginning in 1607 claimed the rights of English citizens, including representative government through bodies like the House of Burgesses..."

moves.move: Move 2 — Show how the 1705 slave codes undermined any claim that those rights extended to everyone.
moves.starter: "However, over the same decades colonists were building their own self-government, colonial law was building the opposite for enslaved people — culminating in the 1705 Virginia slave codes, which declared enslaved people real property with no legal standing as people at all..."

"Unlike later moments in the Thread 1 arc, Unit 11.1 offers no redemption yet — the contradiction between claimed liberty and legal bondage is simply established here, and it will not be addressed even partially until..."

quick_check.heading: Part 6 — Quick Check
quick_check.intro: Try each question yourself before you read the answer underneath it.

items.q: What was salutary neglect, and how did it unintentionally prepare colonists for independence?
items.a: Salutary neglect was Britain's loose enforcement of trade laws and hands-off approach to colonial governance, from the 1600s until 1763. By leaving colonial assemblies to govern themselves for generations, Britain let colonists build real practical self-rule — so when Britain reversed course after 1763, colonists experienced it as the loss of something they already had, not the denial of something new.

items.q: Between 1619 and 1705, what pattern do you see in how colonial law treated enslaved people? Name at least two steps.
items.a: Rights and legal protections were removed one at a time, not all at once. In 1640, John Punch was sentenced to servitude for life while two white servants in the same case received only extra years — the first sign the law was treating Black and white servants differently. In 1662, Virginia ruled a child's status followed the mother's, making enslavement hereditary. By 1705, the process ended with enslaved people declared legal property.

items.q: Why does Bacon's Rebellion (1676) sit in the middle of that pattern, not outside it?
items.a: In 1676, poor whites and enslaved/indentured Black Virginians rebelled together against the colony's elite. That alliance showed Virginia's elite what the two groups could do if they had shared interests — and the colony's response afterward accelerated the shift toward race-based slavery, deliberately separating groups the law had, until then, treated more similarly.

items.q: What did the 1705 Virginia slave codes declare enslaved people to legally be? Why does that word choice matter?
items.a: The 1705 codes declared enslaved people to be real property — legally real estate, not people. That word choice matters because it moved slavery from a status a person held, like an indentured servant's temporary contract, to a category of ownership with no legal end and no legal personhood at all.

items.q: Name the primary Regents Thread for Unit 11.1 and write one sentence connecting the 1705 slave codes to it.
items.a: Thread 1 — Is There One America? The 1705 slave codes are the earliest entry in the Thread 1 arc: the same colonial world claiming the rights of Englishmen for itself defined enslaved people as property under the law, and that contradiction is not resolved anywhere in this unit.
